case_analysis.focal_point: Whether federal courts of appeals have jurisdiction to review the 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' determination in cancellation of removal cases as a 'question of law' under 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2)(D), specifically whether the application of a legal standard to established facts constitutes a reviewable mixed question of law and fact.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 8 U.S.C. § 1252(a)(2)(D), which preserves federal court jurisdiction to review 'questions of law' arising from immigration agency decisions even when other statutory provisions limit or eliminate judicial review, in conjunction with the cancellation of removal provisions under the Immigration and Nationality Act requiring a showing of 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' to a qualifying relative.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioner Situ Kamu Wilkinson argues that under the Supreme Court's binding precedent in Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr (2020), the application of the 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' legal standard to established facts constitutes a mixed question of law and fact that qualifies as a reviewable 'question of law' under § 1252(a)(2)(D). Petitioner contends that the Third Circuit erred in holding it lacked jurisdiction to review the BIA's hardship determination, as Guerrero-Lasprilla categorically established that federal courts may review immigration judges' application of any legal standard to established facts. Petitioner further argues, supported by multiple amici including domestic violence survivor organizations and former immigration judges, that meaningful judicial review is essential to ensure fair adjudication, correct legal errors, and prevent arbitrary and inconsistent application of immigration law standards that disproportionately harm vulnerable populations including domestic violence survivors.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Attorney General Merrick Garland, as Respondent, argues that the 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' determination is a discretionary, fact-intensive, and inherently subjective judgment that falls outside the scope of reviewable 'questions of law' under § 1252(a)(2)(D). The government's position, as characterized by Petitioner and amici, attempts to carve out an exception to Guerrero-Lasprilla's categorical rule by categorizing certain statutory standards as too discretionary, subjective, or judgment-laden to constitute legal questions amenable to appellate review, effectively arguing that the hardship determination is a pure exercise of agency discretion insulated from judicial scrutiny.
key_precedents: Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr, 140 S. Ct. 1062 (2020) - established that mixed questions of law and fact, including application of legal standards to established facts, constitute reviewable 'questions of law' under § 1252(a)(2)(D)
Patel v. Garland, 142 S. Ct. 1614 (2022) - addressed scope of judicial review in immigration cases and limits on factual review

Ray Haluch Gravel Co. v. Central Pension Fund of International Union of Operating Engineers & Participating Employers, 571 U.S. 177 (2014) - cited for the principle that bright-line jurisdictional rules should not be undermined by carving out implicit exceptions, preserving operational consistency and predictability
Tacuri-Tacuri v. Garland, 998 F.3d 466 (1st Cir. 2021) - illustrating circuit court difficulties in distinguishing factual challenges from legal ones in cancellation of removal cases
Alvarado v. Holder, 743 F.3d 271 (1st Cir. 2014) - demonstrating jurisdictional ambiguity in hardship determinations across circuits
Romero-Torres v. Ashcroft, 327 F.3d 887 (9th Cir. 2003) - addressing jurisdictional limits on reviewing subjective immigration standards such as 'good moral character'
Hertz Corp. v. Friend, 559 U.S. 77 (2010) - cited in support of the principle that clear jurisdictional rules prevent the type of confusion and 'mental gymnastics' that vague boundaries create

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious challenge to my position, arguing from original public meaning that 'questions of law' would not naturally encompass the highly discretionary 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' determination. This is a genuinely weighty textualist argument, and I acknowledge that Guerrero-Lasprilla's categorical rule may have swept more broadly than I would have preferred had I been writing on a clean slate. However, my commitment to institutional legitimacy and stare decisis counsels strongly against creating exceptions to a categorical rule this Court established just four years ago — as Justice Kavanaugh correctly notes, allowing the government to relitigate settled jurisdictional questions circuit-by-circuit would undermine both the rule of law and this Court's credibility. The narrow grounds I prefer here are simply faithful application of Guerrero-Lasprilla's existing framework rather than crafting new exceptions, and as Chief Justice I would assign a majority opinion that applies that precedent without unnecessarily expanding it, leaving open questions about the appropriate scope of appellate deference to agency expertise on the underlying factual judgments.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: After further reflection on my colleagues' arguments, I maintain my reluctant position with the petitioner, though my confidence remains modest. Justice Barrett's point about the original public meaning of 'questions of law' in appellate review contexts — that it has historically encompassed whether a decision-maker correctly applied a legal standard to established facts — is the argument that most moves me, because it engages my originalist methodology directly rather than simply invoking stare decisis. However, I write separately to emphasize what my colleagues have not sufficiently grappled with: the distinction between reviewing whether an agency correctly understood a legal standard versus reviewing the agency's exercise of judgment in applying that standard to facts is not merely semantic — Congress's explicit stripping of review in § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i) for 'judgment or discretion' determinations must be given independent operative effect, and courts of appeals exercising jurisdiction under § 1252(a)(2)(D) must be scrupulous not to allow 'questions of law' review to become a backdoor for substituting judicial for agency judgment on the inherently discretionary hardship weighing. Justice Gorsuch's separation of powers argument, while compelling in the abstract, does not fully answer my concern that Article III courts substituting their judgment for agency expertise on fact-intensive discretionary determinations raises its own separation of powers problems — the principle cuts in both directions, and the appropriate resolution is jurisdiction with robust deference, not jurisdiction with de novo review of the hardship calculus.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas's argument from original public meaning remains the most intellectually honest challenge to this position, and I continue to believe he was correct in his Guerrero-Lasprilla dissent that 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' is more akin to a discretionary weighing exercise than a traditional 'question of law.' However, as I noted in my initial reasoning, stare decisis constrains me here in a way that Justice Thomas himself ultimately acknowledges — his own dissent characterized Guerrero-Lasprilla's holding as categorical in scope, and I cannot in good conscience carve out an ad hoc exception that the statute's text does not support and that our four-year-old precedent forecloses. Justice Kagan correctly observes that the government's proposed distinction between 'subjective' and 'objective' legal standards is precisely the kind of sliding-scale approach Guerrero-Lasprilla rejected, and permitting that distinction to do jurisdictional work would recreate the circuit inconsistency the categorical rule was designed to prevent. I maintain my position while noting, as I did in joining Justice Thomas's original dissent, that Guerrero-Lasprilla's broad sweep may warrant future reconsideration in an appropriate case.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious challenge, arguing from original public meaning that 'questions of law' would not naturally encompass the highly discretionary 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' determination. But this argument, however methodologically coherent, runs directly into the categorical holding of Guerrero-Lasprilla, which Justice Thomas himself acknowledged in dissent was sweeping in scope — and stare decisis demands we apply that precedent consistently rather than selectively. The government's proposed carve-out for 'discretionary' standards is precisely what Guerrero-Lasprilla foreclosed when it rejected the sliding-scale alternative, and as Justice Kagan correctly notes, § 1252(a)(2)(D)'s text contains no exception for judgment-laden standards. Beyond the doctrinal analysis, the real-world stakes reinforce my position: permitting agencies to insulate hardship determinations from all judicial review would leave domestic violence survivors and other vulnerable noncitizens without any meaningful check on arbitrary or legally erroneous agency action — exactly the kind of consequence that should give us pause before reading jurisdictional limitations broadly.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious challenge to our position, arguing that the original public meaning of 'questions of law' would not encompass the highly discretionary 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' determination. But this argument, while methodologically coherent, runs directly into the categorical holding of Guerrero-Lasprilla, which Thomas himself acknowledged in dissent was sweeping in scope — and stare decisis binds us to that precedent regardless of whether we might have decided it differently. The government's proposed carve-out for 'subjective' or 'discretionary' standards is precisely the kind of implicit exception-carving that Guerrero-Lasprilla rejected when it declined the sliding-scale alternative, and as I noted in my initial analysis, permitting such case-by-case exceptions would recreate the circuit inconsistency and 'mental gymnastics' that bright-line jurisdictional rules are designed to prevent. Justice Alito's point about appropriate deference to agency expertise on underlying factual judgments is well-taken and can be incorporated into how courts of appeals exercise this jurisdiction — but it does not affect whether jurisdiction exists in the first place under § 1252(a)(2)(D).

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious challenge to my position, arguing from originalist grounds that 'questions of law' as originally understood would not encompass the highly discretionary 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' determination. I take this argument seriously as a fellow originalist, but I find it ultimately unpersuasive for two reasons: first, Guerrero-Lasprilla's categorical holding — which Justice Thomas himself acknowledged in dissent was categorical in scope — is now binding precedent, and stare decisis demands I apply it consistently rather than selectively; second, and more fundamentally, the distinction Justice Thomas draws between 'more defined' legal standards like equitable tolling and 'vaguer' standards like hardship finds no foothold in the text of § 1252(a)(2)(D), which preserves review of 'questions of law' without qualification. As I noted in my initial reasoning, allowing the Executive Branch to insulate its legal determinations from Article III review by simply labeling them 'discretionary' or 'judgment-laden' would represent precisely the kind of unchecked agency power that separation of powers principles counsel against — the vagueness of a standard does not transform its application into a purely factual exercise immune from legal correction. Justice Alito's observation that courts of appeals should exercise this jurisdiction with appropriate deference to underlying factual judgments is well-taken and provides a workable limiting principle that addresses the government's practical concerns without creating an unprincipled jurisdictional carve-out.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas makes the strongest opposing argument by invoking original public meaning of 'questions of law' and contending that 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' is fundamentally a discretionary weighing exercise that Congress intended to insulate from review — a position he articulated in his Guerrero-Lasprilla dissent. However, as I noted in my initial reasoning, the majority in Guerrero-Lasprilla explicitly considered and rejected the argument that certain standards are too judgment-laden for appellate review, and stare decisis demands that we honor that categorical holding rather than relitigate it through case-by-case exceptions. Justice Thomas's textualist and originalist methodology is internally consistent, but the practical consequence of his approach — allowing the government to insulate legal determinations from Article III review simply by characterizing them as discretionary — would undermine the separation of powers values that even originalists should find troubling. As Chief Justice Roberts correctly observes, institutional legitimacy is best served by consistent application of our own recent precedent, and Guerrero-Lasprilla's four-year-old categorical rule should not be eroded through circuit-by-circuit carve-outs that the Court already foreclosed.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious challenge to my position, arguing from originalist premises that 'questions of law' as originally understood would not encompass the highly discretionary 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' determination. I take this argument seriously as a fellow originalist, but I find it ultimately unpersuasive for two reasons: first, Guerrero-Lasprilla's categorical holding — which even Justice Thomas acknowledged in dissent was categorical in scope — forecloses the distinction he draws between more and less 'defined' legal standards, and stare decisis requires me to apply that precedent consistently rather than selectively; second, the original public meaning of 'questions of law' in appellate review contexts has long encompassed whether a decision-maker correctly applied a legal standard to established facts, which is precisely what courts of appeals would review here without disturbing underlying factual findings. Justice Gorsuch's point about separation of powers further reinforces my view: allowing the Executive Branch to insulate its own legal determinations from Article III review simply by labeling them 'discretionary' would permit a structural end-run around Congress's explicit preservation of jurisdiction in § 1252(a)(2)(D). The near-unanimity of my colleagues on this point reflects not groupthink but the genuine strength of the textual and precedential case for the petitioner.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious challenge, arguing that 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' is so discretionary and judgment-laden that it falls outside the original public meaning of 'questions of law' — and I take seriously his point that Guerrero-Lasprilla's categorical rule may sweep too broadly. However, even accepting that the hardship standard involves significant agency discretion, the question before us is not whether courts should second-guess the weight the BIA assigns to particular facts, but whether the BIA correctly understood and applied the legal standard itself — and that is unambiguously a question of law under Guerrero-Lasprilla's categorical holding. The government's proposed carve-out for 'subjective' or 'discretionary' standards has no textual anchor in § 1252(a)(2)(D) and would require courts to engage in precisely the case-by-case jurisdictional parsing that Guerrero-Lasprilla rejected when it declined the government's sliding-scale alternative. From my perspective as a former public defender, I am acutely aware that insulating hardship determinations from any legal review — particularly in cases involving domestic violence survivors — would leave the most vulnerable noncitizens without recourse when agencies misapply or misunderstand the governing legal standard, which is a consequence Congress did not intend when it preserved 'questions of law' in § 1252(a)(2)(D).

John Roberts.reasoning: Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr, 140 S. Ct. 1062 (2020), established a categorical rule that the application of a legal standard to established facts constitutes a reviewable 'question of law' under § 1252(a)(2)(D), and as Justice Thomas noted in dissent, the majority's holding was explicitly categorical in scope. The government's attempt to carve out an exception for 'discretionary' or 'subjective' standards like 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' finds no textual support in § 1252(a)(2)(D) and would undermine the bright-line jurisdictional clarity this Court has consistently valued, as reflected in Hertz Corp. v. Friend and Ray Haluch Gravel Co. My preference for narrow rulings counsels applying Guerrero-Lasprilla's existing framework rather than creating new exceptions, and institutional legitimacy is best served by consistent application of our own recent precedent rather than allowing the circuits to develop conflicting jurisdictional rules around the same statutory provision.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: While I dissented in Guerrero-Lasprilla precisely because I believed the majority's categorical rule was overbroad and texturally unsound, stare decisis considerations and the majority's own categorical language create tension here. However, applying my originalist and textualist methodology to § 1252(a)(2)(D), the phrase 'questions of law' as understood at the time of enactment would not naturally encompass the highly discretionary, judgment-laden 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' determination, which is fundamentally a weighing of facts against a vague statutory standard rather than a legal question amenable to appellate correction. As I noted in my Guerrero-Lasprilla dissent, the majority's categorical rule sweeps too broadly and effectively nullifies Congress's deliberate jurisdictional limitations, and the 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' standard—unlike equitable tolling's more defined legal contours—represents precisely the kind of discretionary agency judgment Congress intended to insulate from judicial review under § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i). The original public meaning of 'questions of law' supports a narrower reading that preserves meaningful limits on federal court jurisdiction consistent with Congress's structural design.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: As a textualist, I must apply § 1252(a)(2)(D) as written, and Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr, 140 S. Ct. 1062 (2020) established a categorical rule — acknowledged even by the dissenters — that 'questions of law' encompasses mixed questions including the application of legal standards to established facts. While I am skeptical of expansive judicial review that second-guesses agency discretion in immigration matters, and I find the government's argument that 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' is a highly discretionary, judgment-laden standard to have considerable force, the text of § 1252(a)(2)(D) does not carve out exceptions for particularly discretionary standards, and Guerrero-Lasprilla's holding does not permit courts to create such implicit exceptions. The principle from Hertz Corp. v. Friend and Ray Haluch Gravel Co. that bright-line jurisdictional rules should not be undermined by ad hoc exceptions counsels against the government's proposed case-by-case carve-out, even if I might have decided Guerrero-Lasprilla differently. Stare decisis and textual fidelity require applying the categorical rule established in Guerrero-Lasprilla to the hardship determination here, though courts of appeals should exercise this jurisdiction with appropriate deference to agency expertise on the underlying factual judgments.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr, 140 S. Ct. 1062 (2020), established a categorical rule that the application of any legal standard to established facts constitutes a reviewable 'question of law' under § 1252(a)(2)(D) — a holding so broad that even the dissenting Justices acknowledged its categorical scope. The government's attempt to carve out the 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' determination as too discretionary or subjective to constitute a legal question is precisely the kind of case-by-case exception this Court rejected in Guerrero-Lasprilla when it declined the government's alternative argument for a sliding-scale analysis. Permitting such an exception would undermine the clear jurisdictional rule the Court established, create the very circuit confusion and 'mental gymnastics' that Hertz Corp. v. Friend warns against, and — critically — leave vulnerable populations including domestic violence survivors without meaningful judicial recourse to correct arbitrary or legally erroneous agency determinations. The practical reality that hardship determinations disproportionately affect the most marginalized noncitizens makes robust judicial review not merely permissible but essential to the fair administration of immigration law.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr established a categorical rule that mixed questions of law and fact — including the application of any legal standard to established facts — constitute reviewable 'questions of law' under § 1252(a)(2)(D), and the government's attempt to carve out an exception for 'discretionary' or 'subjective' standards is precisely the kind of implicit exception-carving the Court rejected in that decision. As a pragmatic textualist, I find that the statutory text of § 1252(a)(2)(D) preserving review of 'questions of law' admits no categorical exclusion for standards that happen to be judgment-laden; the 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' standard is still a legal standard whose application to established facts is reviewable. Allowing courts of appeals to review whether the BIA correctly applied this standard — without second-guessing underlying factual findings — is both workable and consistent with the coherent jurisdictional framework Congress designed in § 1252. Permitting the government's proposed case-by-case discretionary carve-out would recreate exactly the 'mental gymnastics' and circuit inconsistency that Guerrero-Lasprilla and Hertz Corp. v. Friend counsel against, undermining the operational predictability that bright-line jurisdictional rules are meant to provide.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The plain text of § 1252(a)(2)(D) preserves jurisdiction over 'questions of law,' and this Court's decision in Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr categorically established that mixed questions of law and fact — including the application of a legal standard to established facts — constitute reviewable 'questions of law' under that provision. The government's attempt to carve out an exception for 'discretionary' or 'judgment-laden' standards was precisely the kind of case-by-case jurisdictional parsing that Guerrero-Lasprilla rejected, and the dissenters in that case themselves acknowledged the majority's rule was categorical. As a textualist, I am bound by what Congress wrote in § 1252(a)(2)(D), and nothing in that text supports reading an implicit exception for standards deemed too subjective for judicial review — such ad hoc line-drawing would undermine the operational consistency and predictability that clear jurisdictional rules demand, as we recognized in Ray Haluch Gravel Co. The rule of lenity and separation of powers concerns further counsel against allowing the Executive Branch to insulate its own legal determinations from Article III review by simply labeling them discretionary.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr (2020) established a categorical rule that mixed questions of law and fact — including the application of legal standards to established facts — constitute reviewable 'questions of law' under § 1252(a)(2)(D), and the Court explicitly rejected both the government's 'pure questions only' argument and a case-by-case balancing approach. The government's attempt here to carve out an exception for 'discretionary,' 'subjective,' or 'judgment-laden' standards is precisely the kind of implicit exception-carving that this Court rejected in Ray Haluch Gravel Co., where we emphasized that bright-line jurisdictional rules must not be undermined by ad hoc exceptions that compromise operational consistency and predictability. As an institutionalist, I am particularly attentive to the importance of courts adhering faithfully to their own recent precedents — Guerrero-Lasprilla was decided only four years ago and the majority's categorical holding was clear enough that even the dissenters (Justices Thomas and Alito) acknowledged its breadth. Allowing the Third Circuit's jurisdictional bar to stand would effectively permit the government to relitigate a settled question through circuit-by-circuit erosion, which undermines both the rule of law and the Court's institutional credibility.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: As a textualist and originalist, I begin with the statutory text of § 1252(a)(2)(D), which preserves jurisdiction over 'questions of law' without carving out exceptions for discretionary or judgment-laden determinations. Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr, 140 S. Ct. 1062 (2020), categorically held that mixed questions of law and fact — including the application of a legal standard to established facts — constitute reviewable 'questions of law' under this provision, and even the dissenters acknowledged the holding's categorical scope. The government's attempt to exempt the 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' standard by characterizing it as too 'subjective' or 'discretionary' for judicial review is precisely the kind of implicit exception-carving that this Court rejected in Ray Haluch Gravel Co., which warned that such maneuvers undermine the operational consistency and predictability that bright-line jurisdictional rules are designed to provide. Methodological consistency demands that I apply Guerrero-Lasprilla's categorical rule uniformly; to do otherwise would be to rewrite the statute by judicial gloss, substituting my own policy preferences for the text Congress enacted and the precedent this Court has established.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr, 140 S. Ct. 1062 (2020), established a categorical rule that the application of any legal standard to established facts constitutes a reviewable 'question of law' under § 1252(a)(2)(D) — a characterization acknowledged even by the dissenters. The government's attempt to carve out an exception for 'discretionary' or 'subjective' standards like 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' is precisely the kind of case-by-case jurisdictional parsing that Guerrero-Lasprilla expressly rejected when it declined the government's alternative argument for a more-factual-or-more-legal sliding scale analysis. Allowing such an exception would undermine the predictability and consistency that clear jurisdictional rules require, as reinforced by Hertz Corp. v. Friend and Ray Haluch Gravel Co., and would insulate from meaningful review agency determinations that disproportionately affect vulnerable populations — including domestic violence survivors — in ways that raise serious procedural fairness and equal protection concerns. The Third Circuit's jurisdictional holding cannot stand when it conflicts with this Court's binding categorical precedent.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious counterargument — that § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i)'s specific jurisdiction-stripping language for 'any judgment regarding the granting of relief' under cancellation of removal should control over the general 'questions of law' preservation in § 1252(a)(2)(D), invoking the canon that specific provisions govern over general ones. This is a genuinely weighty structural argument that I must take seriously. However, the better reading is that § 1252(a)(2)(D) was enacted precisely to restore some judicial oversight that § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i) had stripped, and Guerrero-Lasprilla's categorical holding already resolved this tension by establishing that mixed questions of law and fact survive the jurisdiction-stripping provisions as 'questions of law' — the Court was well aware that cancellation of removal determinations were among the affected decisions. My minimalist instincts counsel that the narrowest and most institutionally sound path is faithful application of Guerrero-Lasprilla's categorical rule rather than creating an implicit exception that would require case-by-case jurisdictional determinations, and as Chief Justice I would assign the majority opinion with language that emphasizes the limited scope of appellate review — courts assess only whether the legal standard was correctly applied to established facts, not substitute their own factual judgments — which should preserve the institutional legitimacy concerns Justice Thomas and I share while honoring our recent precedent.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch and Justice Barrett make the decisive textual point that I cannot escape: § 1252(a)(2)(D) was enacted specifically to carve back jurisdiction from § 1252(a)(2)(B)'s stripping provisions, which means the specific-over-general canon actually cuts against the government's position — § 1252(a)(2)(D) is the more specific provision as applied to legal questions, operating as a targeted exception to the exception. My own dissent in Guerrero-Lasprilla acknowledged the majority's categorical proclamation that federal courts may review immigration judges' applications of any legal standard to established facts, and intellectual honesty requires me to apply that holding here even as I continue to believe it was wrongly decided. Justice Barrett correctly identifies that the hardship determination's discretionary character is a merits question about the appropriate standard of review, not a jurisdictional question — and conflating the two would require us to effectively overrule or substantially limit Guerrero-Lasprilla, which the parties have not squarely asked us to do. I therefore join the petitioner's position while preserving my view that Guerrero-Lasprilla was incorrectly decided and that a future case presenting the right vehicle should reconsider whether § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i)'s specific jurisdiction-stripping language should control over § 1252(a)(2)(D) for purely discretionary agency judgments.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas's reluctant concession is the most significant development in this round — his acknowledgment that Guerrero-Lasprilla's categorical holding, which he himself helped define through his dissent, forecloses the government's standard-by-standard exception without a direct request to overrule that precedent, confirms that even the strongest textualist argument against jurisdiction cannot survive honest engagement with binding precedent. I agree with Justice Barrett that the specific-over-general canon cannot swallow § 1252(a)(2)(D) entirely, because that provision was enacted precisely to carve back legal questions from § 1252(a)(2)(B)'s jurisdiction-stripping — rendering it a restoration clause that is itself the more specific provision as applied to questions of law. My practical concerns about courts second-guessing inherently discretionary agency hardship determinations are real, but as Justice Kavanaugh correctly notes, those concerns go to the appropriate standard of review on the merits, not to the threshold jurisdictional question. The near-unanimous convergence across methodological commitments — from Justice Sotomayor's purposivism to Justice Gorsuch's textualism to Justice Thomas's reluctant originalism — reinforces that the text, structure, and binding precedent of Guerrero-Lasprilla compel jurisdiction here, and I write separately only to emphasize that courts of appeals must exercise this jurisdiction with appropriate deference to the agency's factual judgments.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious counterargument — that § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i)'s specific jurisdiction-stripping language for 'any judgment regarding the granting of relief' under cancellation of removal should control over the general 'questions of law' preservation in § 1252(a)(2)(D). But this argument was available to the government in Guerrero-Lasprilla and the Court's categorical holding implicitly addressed it: § 1252(a)(2)(D) was enacted precisely to restore some judicial review that § 1252(a)(2)(B) had stripped, and reading (D) to yield entirely to (B)(i) whenever a discretionary standard is involved would render (D)'s preservation meaningless in the immigration cancellation context. As Justice Kagan correctly notes, the question here is not whether courts reweigh facts but whether the agency correctly applied a legal standard — that is the core of what Guerrero-Lasprilla held reviewable, and the 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' standard is no different in kind from equitable tolling, which also involves judgment-laden application of a legal standard to facts. From my pragmatic perspective, the documented inconsistency in hardship determinations — particularly affecting domestic violence survivors — makes judicial review not merely permissible but essential to ensure the legal standard is applied coherently rather than arbitrarily.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious counterargument — that § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i)'s specific jurisdiction-stripping language for 'any judgment regarding the granting of relief' under cancellation of removal should control over the general 'questions of law' preservation in § 1252(a)(2)(D), invoking the specific-over-general canon. But this argument was available to the government in Guerrero-Lasprilla and the Court's categorical holding implicitly addressed the relationship between these provisions by establishing that § 1252(a)(2)(D) operates as a restoration clause that carves back out legal questions from whatever § 1252(a)(2)(B) strips away — the two provisions work in tandem, not in conflict. The 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' determination is not a pure discretionary 'judgment' insulated by § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i); it is the application of a congressionally enacted legal standard to facts, which is precisely what Guerrero-Lasprilla held falls within § 1252(a)(2)(D)'s preservation. As Justice Barrett correctly notes, even EOIR treats this as a mixed question subject to de novo review at the BIA level, which confirms that the hardship determination has a legal component amenable to judicial review without transforming courts of appeals into factfinders.

But this argument founders on the text itself: § 1252(a)(2)(D) was enacted precisely to restore judicial review that § 1252(a)(2)(B) stripped, and Congress's deliberate choice to carve back jurisdiction for 'questions of law' from the broader jurisdiction-stripping provision means § 1252(a)(2)(D) is the more specific provision as applied to legal questions — it is a targeted exception to the exception. Guerrero-Lasprilla's categorical holding that mixed questions of law and fact constitute 'questions of law' under § 1252(a)(2)(D) forecloses the Government's attempt to resurrect a sliding-scale approach based on the perceived subjectivity of the hardship standard, and as Justice Barrett correctly notes, the text of § 1252(a)(2)(D) draws no distinction between more or less discretionary legal standards. The near-unanimity of my colleagues across methodological commitments — from Justice Sotomayor's purposivist approach to Justice Barrett's textualism — reinforces that the plain statutory text and binding precedent compel jurisdiction here.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious counterargument by invoking the specific-over-general canon — that § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i)'s targeted jurisdiction-stripping for 'any judgment regarding the granting of relief' under cancellation of removal should control over § 1252(a)(2)(D)'s general 'questions of law' preservation. This is a genuinely weighty structural argument that deserves careful attention. However, Guerrero-Lasprilla itself addressed this precise tension and resolved it by holding that § 1252(a)(2)(D) operates as a restoration provision that carves back out legal questions from the jurisdiction-stripping provisions, including § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i) — the two provisions work in tandem rather than in conflict, with (D) serving as the exception to (B). My institutionalist commitments counsel strongly against creating a judge-made exception to a categorical rule this Court articulated just four years ago, particularly where, as Justice Roberts correctly notes, the government is effectively asking us to relitigate Guerrero-Lasprilla through factual distinctions that the majority opinion's categorical language forecloses. The circuit split on this question further reinforces that a uniform, predictable rule is essential to the Court's institutional role, and the proper resolution is faithful application of our own recent precedent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas raises the most serious counterargument by invoking the specific-over-general canon — that § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i)'s jurisdiction-stripping language for 'any judgment regarding the granting of relief' should control over § 1252(a)(2)(D)'s general 'questions of law' preservation for this particular determination. This is a genuinely weighty structural argument that deserves careful attention. However, § 1252(a)(2)(D) was enacted precisely to restore judicial review that § 1252(a)(2)(B) had stripped, and reading it as categorically preserving 'questions of law' — including mixed questions per Guerrero-Lasprilla — gives full effect to Congress's remedial purpose without rendering § 1252(a)(2)(D) superfluous. The specific-over-general canon cannot swallow a provision Congress enacted specifically to carve back jurisdiction from the broader stripping provisions; otherwise § 1252(a)(2)(D) would have no operative effect in the very cases where it was most needed. I agree with Justice Kavanaugh that the hardship determination's discretionary character goes to the merits of review — specifically the appropriate standard of review — not to whether jurisdiction exists in the first instance.

The government's attempt to carve out the 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' determination as uniquely discretionary is precisely the kind of case-by-case jurisdictional exception this Court rejected in Guerrero-Lasprilla when it declined the government's alternative argument for a more-factual-or-more-legal sliding scale analysis. My minimalist instincts counsel against creating implicit exceptions to clear jurisdictional rules, consistent with Hertz Corp. v. Clarence Thomas.reasoning: While I dissented in Guerrero-Lasprilla precisely because I believed the majority's categorical rule was overbroad and would lead to exactly this kind of jurisdictional expansion, I must now grapple with the consequences of that holding as binding precedent. As the research materials note, I myself acknowledged in dissent that the Guerrero-Lasprilla majority 'categorically proclaims that federal courts may review immigration judges' applications of any legal standard to established facts,' which cuts against the government's position here. However, from an originalist and textualist standpoint, the 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' standard is qualitatively different — it is a congressionally delegated discretionary judgment, and the text of § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i) specifically strips jurisdiction over 'any judgment regarding the granting of relief' under the cancellation of removal provisions, suggesting Congress intended to insulate this particular determination from review. The structural canon that specific provisions control over general ones, combined with Congress's evident intent to vest discretionary hardship determinations in the agency, counsels that § 1252(a)(2)(B)(i)'s specific jurisdiction-stripping language should prevail over the general 'questions of law' preservation in § 1252(a)(2)(D) for this uniquely discretionary standard.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: As a textualist, I must acknowledge that § 1252(a)(2)(D) preserves jurisdiction over 'questions of law,' and this Court's holding in Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr, 140 S. Ct. 1062 (2020), categorically established that mixed questions of law and fact — specifically the application of a legal standard to established facts — constitute reviewable 'questions of law' under that provision. The dissent in Guerrero-Lasprilla itself acknowledged the majority's holding was categorical, which forecloses the government's attempt to carve out an implicit exception for the 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' standard based on its allegedly more subjective or discretionary character. While I have reservations about expanding judicial oversight of immigration agency determinations and am sympathetic to the government's concern that this standard involves inherently discretionary judgment, the text of § 1252(a)(2)(D) as authoritatively construed in Guerrero-Lasprilla does not permit courts to selectively disclaim jurisdiction based on the perceived subjectivity of the legal standard at issue. Consistent with the principle from Hertz Corp. v. Friend that clear jurisdictional rules should not be undermined by implicit exceptions, I would hold that the Third Circuit retains jurisdiction to review the hardship determination as a mixed question of law and fact.

Ct. 1062 (2020), established a categorical rule that 'questions of law' under § 1252(a)(2)(D) include mixed questions of law and fact — specifically, the application of a legal standard to established facts — and even the dissenting Justices acknowledged this holding was categorical in scope. The government's attempt to carve out the 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' standard as uniquely discretionary and therefore unreviewable was precisely the kind of case-by-case, standard-by-standard exception that Guerrero-Lasprilla explicitly rejected when it dismissed the government's alternative argument for a sliding-scale approach to mixed questions. Allowing courts of appeals to review whether the BIA correctly applied the hardship standard to established facts does not transform them into factfinders; it ensures the legal standard is applied consistently and not arbitrarily — a concern of acute importance given the documented inconsistency in hardship determinations affecting domestic violence survivors and other vulnerable populations. Permitting the government's proposed exception would also undermine the bright-line jurisdictional clarity that Hertz Corp. v. Friend and Ray Haluch Gravel Co. counsel us to preserve.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Guerrero-Lasprilla v. Barr squarely established that 'questions of law' under § 1252(a)(2)(D) include mixed questions of law and fact — specifically the application of a legal standard to established facts — and the Court explicitly rejected both the government's categorical exclusion of mixed questions and its proposed case-by-case subjectivity analysis. The 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' standard is precisely such a mixed question: courts of appeals are not being asked to reweigh raw facts, but to assess whether the agency correctly applied a statutory legal standard to undisputed facts, which is the core of what Guerrero-Lasprilla held reviewable. Allowing the government to carve out an exception for 'particularly subjective' standards would resurrect the very case-by-case jurisdictional analysis Guerrero-Lasprilla rejected, undermining the workability and predictability that clear jurisdictional rules require, as reinforced by Hertz Corp. v. Friend. From a pragmatic standpoint, permitting review also serves the statutory purpose of § 1252(a)(2)(D) — ensuring legal coherence and uniform application of immigration standards — without transforming courts of appeals into factfinders, since they would review only whether the legal standard was correctly applied, not substitute their own factual judgments.

The Government's attempt to carve out an exception for the 'exceptional and extremely unusual hardship' standard because it is purportedly more 'discretionary' or 'subjective' was precisely the kind of case-by-case jurisdictional parsing that Guerrero-Lasprilla rejected; the Court there refused both the 'pure questions only' reading and the sliding-scale approach the Government now effectively resurrects. As a textualist, I am bound by what the statute says, not by what the agency finds convenient, and nothing in § 1252(a)(2)(D)'s text supports an implicit carve-out for standards deemed too judgment-laden — a rule that would swallow the jurisdictional preservation Congress enacted. Consistent with the principle from Hertz Corp. v. Friend that clear jurisdictional rules must not be undermined by ad hoc exceptions, the Third Circuit erred in declining jurisdiction.
